statement: In a 20-day residential laboratory study of 8 volunteers with stimulant experience, measured total daily food intake fell by about 43% after a sampled 5 mg oral dose of methamphetamine and by about 37% after a 10 mg dose, relative to the matched placebo conditions (both P<0.01), with no selective effect on fat, carbohydrate or protein; the authors give an average reduction of about 1415 kcal. Intake fell through fewer eating occasions and longer gaps between them at the smaller dose and through smaller meals at the larger one, and ratings of hunger were lower after the 10 mg dose (11.46 against 26.50 on a 0–100 scale). The absolute intakes appear only in a figure, the smaller dose produced the larger percentage reduction, and this is a single study of 8 people (Hart et al., 2001).
plain: In a study where people lived in a laboratory and every item they ate was recorded, a single oral dose of meth cut what they ate that day by roughly a third to a half compared with a dummy capsule, and they said they felt less hungry. It is one small study of eight people, and the actual calorie figures are only shown in a graph.
population: Adults with stimulant experience living in a residential laboratory, not seeking treatment (8 volunteers: 1 woman, 7 men)
exposure: A single sampled oral dose of methamphetamine (study conditions: 5 mg and 10 mg capsules)
comparator: Placebo capsules in the same participants, double-blind, with the order of the two active doses counterbalanced
outcome: Total daily caloric intake measured by continuous food recording; number of eating occasions and intake per occasion; hunger ratings
magnitude: About −43% of total daily calories at 5 mg and −37% at 10 mg against the matched placebo conditions (both P<0.01); an average reduction of about 1415 kcal is given in the discussion. Hunger rating 11.46 (SEM 3.94) against 26.50 (SEM 7.18) after the 10 mg dose. Absolute intakes are shown only in Figure 4.

evidence.extracted: Relative to the matched placebo conditions, total daily caloric intake fell by about 43% after the 5 mg and about 37% after the 10 mg sample dose (P<0.01), with fat, carbohydrate and protein falling in parallel; the smaller dose worked through fewer eating occasions and longer gaps between them, the larger through a smaller mean intake per occasion (both P<0.01). Absolute intakes appear only in the figure.
After the 10 mg sample dose, the hunger rating was 11.46 (SEM 3.94) against 26.50 (SEM 7.18) under the matched placebo, one of the items the paper reports as significantly reduced.

evidence.locator: Discussion, paragraph beginning 'As expected, methamphetamine produced substantial decreases'
evidence.extracted: The discussion states an average reduction of about 1415 kcal relative to the placebo conditions and refers to an earlier study from the same laboratory in which repeated 5 mg and 10 mg doses reduced daily intake by about 1150 and 1450 kcal; those earlier figures are second-hand here.

risk_of_bias.note: RoB 2 high overall, mainly for reporting: only significant items of a 50-item scale tabulated, F values without degrees of freedom, an unexplained P<0.03 threshold and no protocol. The food measure itself is objective and validated against the daily trash.

inconsistency.note: Single study; the two doses agree in direction, although the smaller produced the larger percentage reduction.

imprecision.note: 8 participants; no confidence intervals, and the absolute intakes are only in a figure.

grade.reasoning: A double-blind within-person comparison with counterbalanced dose order starts high (METHODS §6.3). Risk of bias −1 for the reporting problems recorded on the card, although the outcome itself is measured rather than self-estimated. Imprecision −1: eight participants, no intervals, values only in a figure. The causal verb is used because the comparison is within person, double-blind and placebo-controlled; the size of the reduction is much less certain than its direction, and the absence of a dose ordering is stated. Strict reading: the magnitude of the reduction is very low certainty: it rests on percentages whose baselines are shown only in a figure.

changelog.change: New draft claim from Hart et al. (2001), read in full. Reduced food intake is among the best-measured acute effects of methamphetamine and no claim covered it; section 5 holds the acute-effect claims. Anchors ai-located by the first reader and not yet checked.
